lead: A yacht is a small home that heels, carries its own gas, water and electricity, and has nowhere to pop out to. A few habits keep it safe and pleasant for everyone on board.

qa.q: What should I do if I smell gas on a boat?
qa.a: No flames, and touch no electrical switch, since a switch makes a spark. Turn the gas off at the bottle, get everyone into fresh air and tell the skipper: bottled gas is **heavier than air** and collects in the bilge.

blocks.p: Bottled cooking gas is **heavier than air**. If it leaks it does not blow away: it sinks into the bilge and stays there, and one spark can set it off. Every gas habit on board follows from that.

lines: Solenoid off: no gas reaches the stove

list: The gas passes three valves: the one on the bottle, the **solenoid** (an electric valve with a switch near the galley) and the burner knob. All three must be open for the stove to light.
Strike the match or lighter first, then open the burner, so that no unburnt gas escapes.
After cooking close the burner and turn the gas off at the solenoid or the bottle. Then no gas sits in the pipe overnight.

blocks.p: **You smell gas**: no flames, and touch no electrical switch, because a switch makes a spark. Turn the gas off at the bottle, get everyone into fresh air and tell the skipper.
Cooking at sea: let the stove swing on its **gimbals** so the pans stay level, clip on the galley strap to keep both hands free, and wear oilskin trousers against scalds.

sections.title: A pump, narrow pipes and one rule

qa.q: What can I put down the toilet on a yacht?
qa.a: Only what you have eaten first, and toilet paper; everything else goes in the bin. The **heads** pump through narrow pipes and block easily, so keep pumping after the bowl looks clean to clear the pipe.

blocks.p: The marine toilet, the **heads**, pumps through narrow pipes and blocks easily. Nothing goes down it that you have not eaten first, except toilet paper. Everything else goes in the bin.

blocks.p: When the bowl looks clean the waste is still in the pipe, so pump on for a while. Under sail a bowl below the waterline can **siphon** sea water in through open seacocks and flood the boat: many skippers want them closed after every use.

sections.title: The tanks and batteries are all you have

qa.q: How long will the yacht's battery last with the engine off?
qa.a: Divide its amp-hours by the amps everything switched on draws: 120 Ah at 8 A lasts 15 hours. With the engine off and no shore power nothing charges the **house battery**, so switch off what nobody uses.

blocks.p: Away from a marina nobody refills the water tanks. Turn the tap off while you soap your hands, the dishes or yourself, and rinse briefly. To see what you can afford, divide what is left by the crew and by the days.

With the engine off and no shore power nothing charges the **house battery**. It holds amp-hours (Ah); everything switched on draws amps (A). Add up the amps, divide the amp-hours by them and you have the hours left. Switch off lights and chargers nobody is using.

qa.q: What does "stow for sea" mean on a sailing yacht?
qa.a: That nothing can move and no water can get below: to **stow for sea**, put loose things in lockers or wedge them, shut hatches and portholes, latch lockers and drawers, and coil lines clear of feet.

blocks.p: When the boat heels, anything loose flies across the cabin: it breaks, or it hurts someone. "Stow for sea" means that nothing can move and no water can get below.

head: What
Before you sail
rows: In a locker, or wedged so they cannot move
Shut, and they stay shut under way
Coiled and stowed clear of feet, none over the side
Bagged and kept aboard for the bins ashore

blocks.p: One wave through an open forehatch soaks a cabin. A loose line trips people, and one trailing over the side can foul the propeller. **Plastic never goes overboard**, at sea or at anchor.

qa.q: How can I avoid getting seasick on a sailing trip?
qa.a: Take your tablet before you sail, as the packet says, sleep well, eat lightly and leave the wine alone the evening before. If **seasickness** starts, come on deck into the fresh air and watch the horizon.

blocks.p: Almost everyone is seasick at some time, and it passes. It is much easier to prevent than to cure: take your tablet **before** you sail, as the packet says, sleep well, eat lightly and leave the wine alone the evening before a lumpy crossing.

blocks.cap: The bow moves most; low down amidships the motion is least. The cockpit has fresh air and a horizon.

blocks.p: If you start to feel queasy, come on deck into the fresh air and watch the **horizon**. Below decks it is worse, and worst of all in the forward cabin, where the motion is greatest. Keep warm, sip water, and tell someone how you feel.

qa.q: What should I do when I'm off watch on a night passage?
qa.a: Rest: go below and sleep even if the cockpit is pleasant, because a tired watchkeeper misses things. Come up a few minutes early, dressed and ready, so that the **watch** you relieve gets its full rest.

blocks.p: On an overnight passage the crew splits into **watches**: one group sails the boat while the other rests, for example three hours on and three hours off.

Off watch, your job is to rest. Go below and sleep even if the evening in the cockpit is pleasant: a tired watchkeeper misses things. Come up a few minutes early, dressed and ready, so that the watch you relieve gets its full rest.
